Latent reasoning outperforms text-based reasoning, generalizes to unseen partner model families, and supports answers about partners’ beliefs, desires, and actions.
papers.selection_reason: Continuous latent theory-of-mind tokens for LLM multi-agent coordination directly advances LLM-based reasoning and agentic behavior.
papers.title: ToM2Vec: Continuous Theory-of-Mind Tokens for Multi-Agent Coordination
papers.tldr: ToM2Vec uses continuous latent tokens to represent uncertain partner mental states, improving multi-agent coordination across diverse interaction settings.

papers.abstract: Real-time whole-body humanoid teleoperation remains challenging due to the computational latency introduced by optimization-based retargeting pipelines and future-frame conditioning. Existing motion tracking policies typically require dense reference targets including full joint positions, body-part transformations, and even future frames, which tightly couples the controller to expensive upstream modules. In this work, we present HuMiT, a whole-body teleoperation system built on a unified tracking policy that requires only a compact reference target, consisting of root height, root velocity, and the SE(3) poses of four sparse keypoints at the current frame, yet achieves competitive tracking fidelity compared to methods relying on more diverse reference states including complete joint positions, dense body-part transformations, and even future frames. Experiments show that our policy achieves a communication-to-inference latency of $\sim$20 ms measured between headset streaming and policy output and a video-based optical flow latency of 65 ms (median) across different motion types. We validate the system on a Unitree G1 humanoid, showcasing split-second reactive responses such as catching a tossed ball, as well as coordinated loco-manipulation capabilities. Project page: https://xiaohu-art.github.io/Track/.
authors: Liu Cao
Botian Xu
Ruoqu Chen
Jiajun Liu
Mingzhi Pei
Zihao Wang
Zhongyu Li
Mengdi Xu
bullets: Addresses latency and upstream-module dependence in optimization-based whole-body teleoperation.
Uses a unified tracking policy conditioned on root height, root velocity, and SE(3) poses of four sparse keypoints.
Avoids requiring full joint states, dense body transformations, or future frames.
Reports ~20 ms communication-to-inference latency and 65 ms median video-based optical-flow latency.
Validated on a Unitree G1 with reactive ball catching and coordinated loco-manipulation.
papers.selection_reason: Whole-body humanoid teleoperation via a learned tracking policy with loco-manipulation fits embodied robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: HuMiT: Low-Latency Whole-Body Humanoid Teleoperation via Compact Reference Tracking
papers.tldr: HuMiT enables low-latency whole-body humanoid teleoperation using only compact, current-frame motion references while maintaining competitive tracking fidelity.

papers.abstract: Using an LLM to generate training data for another is among the most general ways to train one, and it remains common practice. Some frontier teams have closed that route for their own models: what comes back is an answer, or a short summary, without the detailed reasoning trace behind it. That is a little ironic: they were themselves built on distilling human knowledge, and distilling an open-source model is still entirely routine; the restriction applies to their own outputs alone. Recent work recovers the hidden reasoning by replaying encrypted blocks across models. It somehow works, but it breaks the providers' terms of service, so it is not something a product can be built on long-term. We built the alternative. We take the context and the teacher's answer as input, and generate the reasoning trace ourselves, in the style of the student's own model family. Training is two-stage, supervised and then adversarial: a generator learns to regenerate the family's own reasoning traces from their context and answer, and a critic learns how real a reasoning trace looks. Applied to a teacher's answer, the generator writes one in the family's style. An independent judge rates how likely traces are to be genuine on a scale from 0 to 1: ours average 0.68, real traces 0.66, and traces selected by the critic from four candidates 0.82. These are authenticity scores, not correctness rates. We test the idea on five benchmarks with everything else held fixed. On general tasks the five training corpora are about the same; on coding, the generated reasoning beats Fable 5's own thinking content. With the same 5,000 questions and the same teacher answers, HumanEval+ improves by 3.7 points and MBPP+ by 7.1 at the final checkpoint, and the MBPP+ lead holds at every checkpoint. We suspect that reasoning written in the student's family style is easier for it to learn from.
authors: Yan Wang
bullets: Addresses the lack of accessible reasoning traces from closed frontier models without relying on prohibited encrypted-trace recovery.
Uses a two-stage supervised and adversarial setup: a generator reconstructs family-style traces, while a critic evaluates their authenticity.
Generated traces received average authenticity scores comparable to real traces; critic-selected traces scored higher.
Across five benchmarks, results were similar on general tasks, while coding performance improved by 3.7 points on HumanEval+ and 7.1 on MBPP+ under matched data and teacher answers.
The authors hypothesize that reasoning in the student model’s own style is easier to learn from; reported scores measure authenticity, not correctness.
papers.selection_reason: LLM reasoning-trace distillation and student-style trace generation are directly relevant to large language model training.
papers.title: TraceForge: Distilling with Your Own Thinking
papers.tldr: TraceForge generates student-style reasoning traces from a teacher’s context and answer, enabling terms-compliant distillation and improving coding performance.

papers.abstract: Cinematic multi-shot video generation requires both narrative planning and iterative refinement. Existing methods either lack narrative reasoning or rely on feed-forward workflows without policy updates. In this paper, we propose CineEvolve, an agentic self-evolution framework for cinematic multi-shot video generation that unifies a Director and a Critic within a single vision-language policy. Emulating real-world filmmaking that couples iterative direction with critical feedback, we train CineEvolve via alternating reinforcement learning, where the Director surfaces flaws to sharpen the Critic, and the updated Critic guides the Director's targeted revisions. To stabilize co-evolution, we introduce Evolutionary GRPO (E-GRPO), leveraging historical anchoring and revision safeguarding to mitigate advantage inflation. Additionally, we contribute CineTraj, a 40K cinematic trajectory dataset spanning creation, critique, and revision. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CineEvolve outperforms existing approaches. Our code will be available at https://github.com/JingZhe-8/CineEvolve.
authors: Jingzhe Zhang
Peixuan Zhang
Genying Li
Bing Ma
Shuchen Weng
Si Li

bullets: Addresses the need for both narrative planning and iterative refinement in multi-shot video generation.
Unifies a Director and Critic in one vision-language policy trained through alternating reinforcement learning.
Introduces Evolutionary GRPO (E-GRPO) with historical anchoring and revision safeguarding to stabilize co-evolution.
Provides CineTraj, a 40K trajectory dataset covering video creation, critique, and revision.
Experiments report improved performance over existing approaches, though specific metrics are not given.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic self-evolution framework for cinematic multi-shot video generation directly targets video generation research.
papers.title: CineEvolve: An Agentic Self-Evolution Framework for Cinematic Multi-Shot Video Generation
papers.tldr: CineEvolve uses an evolving Director–Critic agent pair to iteratively plan, critique, and refine cinematic multi-shot videos.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained multimodal intelligence requires models to both understand a designated region and localize it from language. Existing methods learn these directions with separate objectives and task-specific annotations. We present Generalized CycleGRPO, the first unified reinforcement learning framework coupling region understanding and localization across spatial, temporal, and spatio-temporal domains. Given a region, a multimodal large language model generates candidate descriptions and then localizes each description to reconstruct the input region. Reconstruction overlap provides a verifiable reward for captioning, while individual localization rewards improve the inverse mapping. A common region-space formulation extends this cycle from image masks and boxes to video intervals and timestamped spatial evidence, without reference captions or an external language-model judge during reinforcement learning. In videos, the cycle encourages descriptions that distinguish a target event from similar recurrences. We introduce DOVE (Distinctive Occurrence-level Video-caption Evaluation), a human-verified contrastive benchmark for this temporal distinctiveness. CycleGRPO improves SAMTok's overall gIoU from 57.5% to 68.2% on GroundingSuite and average gIoU from 71.2% to 78.7% on GRES. For temporal tasks, it achieves 51.9% tIoU on Charades and 33.3% Temporal Evidence Coverage on DOVE, compared with 45.6% and 14.8% for the Qwen3-VL initialization. These results establish region-text cycle consistency as a general self-evaluation principle for multimodal understanding and localization. Models, code, and DOVE are available at https://devinxzhang.github.io/Generalized-CycleGRPO-Page/.
authors: Xin Zhang
Haochen Wang
Beibei Lin
Zhaoxiang Zhang
Robby T. Tan
Jason Li
Dacheng Tao
bullets: Addresses the need for models to describe designated regions and localize them from language using a shared objective rather than separate task-specific supervision.
Generates a description for a region, relocalizes that description, and uses reconstruction overlap plus localization rewards for self-verifiable training.
Extends a common region-space formulation to image masks/boxes, video intervals, and timestamped spatial evidence without reference captions or an external judge during RL.
Introduces DOVE, a human-verified benchmark for evaluating whether video descriptions distinguish a target event from similar recurrences.
Reports improved spatial grounding and temporal localization, including 68.2% gIoU on GroundingSuite, 78.7% on GRES, 51.9% tIoU on Charades, and 33.3% Temporal Evidence Coverage on DOVE.
papers.selection_reason: Unified region-text cycle RL for fine-grained multimodal understanding and spatial grounding directly fits MLLM and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Generalized CycleGRPO for Fine-Grained Multimodal Understanding and Grounding
papers.tldr: Generalized CycleGRPO unifies multimodal region understanding and localization through reinforcement learning with region-text cycle consistency across images and videos.

papers.abstract: Long-context continual pre-training (LCCP) is widely used to improve long-context capability, but how its benefits scale with the number of tokens used for LCCP remains unclear. We investigate this question through modeling, monitoring, and validating the benefits of scaling LCCP. First, we establish an empirical additive power law relating long-context performance to model size and the respective token budgets of short-context pre-training and LCCP. Experiments across five model scales and more than one hundred short- and long-context budget configurations show that the fitted law reproduces the observed trends and extrapolates well to held-out model scales. Second, we introduce \textsc{Constant-Last4}, a training and observation protocol that averages the four most recent consecutive checkpoints from a constant-learning-rate run to enable stable monitoring along a single extensible training trajectory. Under this protocol, the same scaling-law form fits well and accurately predicts the LCCP performance trajectory of a 1.22B-parameter model trained on approximately 100B LCCP tokens. Finally, downstream evaluations along this trajectory show continued improvements in long-context performance, with no clear sign of saturation within the evaluated range. These gains persist after both 128K context extension and supervised fine-tuning, with benefits extending to long-context understanding and agentic tasks. Together, these results argue for continuing to scale LCCP rather than stopping early: its gains are stably observable along an extensible trajectory, quantitatively predictable, and transferable to downstream tasks.
authors: Ziqing Qiao
Xiaoyue Xu
Sikui Zhang
Yinuo Xu
Bingxiang He
Chaojun Xiao

bullets: The study examines how long-context performance scales with model size, short-context pre-training tokens, and LCCP token budgets.
It fits an empirical additive power law that reproduces observed trends and extrapolates to held-out model scales.
The Constant-Last4 protocol stabilizes monitoring by averaging the four latest checkpoints from a constant-learning-rate trajectory.
A 1.22B-parameter model’s performance trajectory is accurately predicted while training on approximately 100B LCCP tokens.
Improvements persist after 128K context extension and supervised fine-tuning, benefiting long-context understanding and agentic tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Empirical scaling laws for long-context continual pre-training directly advance long-context LLM methods and continual learning.
papers.title: Don't Stop Long-Context Continual Pre-Training Too Early: An Empirical Scaling Law
papers.tldr: Long-context continual pre-training keeps improving long-context and downstream capabilities without clear saturation in the evaluated range, and its gains can be modeled predictably as training tokens increase.

papers.abstract: Learning loco-manipulation policies requires demonstrations that capture coordinated base and arm motion on the target embodiment. Robot-free interfaces allow demonstrations to be collected independently of the target robot, increasing flexibility but without directly capturing platform-specific commands, proprioception, and body-mounted observations. On-robot teleoperation allows to capture these signals directly, but requires an interface capable of commanding the complete system concurrently. This paper presents LocoPilot, a single-operator bilateral teleoperation and data-collection framework implemented on a 12-DoF Unitree Go2 quadruped equipped with a 6-DoF AgileX Piper L manipulator, an Intel RealSense D435 wrist camera, and an Intel RealSense D405 head camera. A second 6-DoF Piper L arm, used as the leader and two handheld controllers provide simultaneous control of the base, body posture, manipulator, and gripper. The follower arm interaction forces are estimated without a dedicated force/torque sensor and rendered to the operator through a passivity-constrained haptic channel. A ROS~2 pipeline records synchronized multimodal observations together with a unified 11D action shared by teleoperation and policy deployment. Compared to prior work, LocoPilot uniquely unifies robot-in-the-loop legged data collection, force feedback without motion-capture instrumentation, and the same action interface at deployment. We evaluate the interface across multiple loco-manipulation tasks and validate the complete collection-to-deployment pipeline by fine-tuning MolmoAct2 \cite{MOLMO} on pick-and-place demonstrations and deploying on the physical robot without action retargeting or additional inverse kinematics. Code available at: https://github.com/iit-DLSLab/LocoPilot

Giovanni Minelli

Lorenzo Amatucci

Victor Barasuol

bullets: Addresses the challenge of collecting demonstrations that coordinate legged-base and manipulator motion while preserving robot-specific observations and commands.
Uses a leader arm and two handheld controllers to teleoperate a 12-DoF Unitree Go2 with a 6-DoF Piper L arm and onboard cameras.
Estimates interaction forces without a dedicated force/torque sensor and provides passivity-constrained haptic feedback.
Records synchronized multimodal data with a unified 11D action interface shared between teleoperation and deployment.
Demonstrates the full pipeline on multiple tasks, including physical pick-and-place deployment after fine-tuning MolmoAct2 without action retargeting or additional inverse kinematics.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a teleoperation and data-collection framework for loco-manipulation policy learning, including VLA fine-tuning and physical deployment.
papers.title: LocoPilot: Single-Operator Bilateral Teleoperation for Loco-Manipulation Policy Learning
papers.tldr: LocoPilot enables one operator to collect and deploy loco-manipulation policies on a quadruped by simultaneously controlling its base, body, arm, and gripper with bilateral haptic feedback.

papers.abstract: Imitation learning increasingly relies on novice operators, whose demonstrations fall short of experts' in number and inter-trial consistency. Operators act on what they are shown, yet how the rendering of the robot affects their demonstrations, and the policies trained on them, has not been examined. We study this question with PointHand, a teleoperation interface that renders a multi-fingered robot hand as sparse keypoints at its fingertips and joints, the same keypoints a policy can observe. In a simulated mug-in-box task, 18 novices and 4 experts collected 2,200 trials under three renderings: the real shape of the hand, all keypoints emphasized, or the thumb and index finger alone emphasized. The novices shown the thumb and index finger emphasized collected 441 successful demonstrations from 600 trials, against 320 for those shown the real shape. We then trained diffusion policies on these demonstrations, replacing the scene point cloud and proprioceptive state they observe with the hand keypoints and two object keypoints. Within 400 steps these demonstrations went from the weakest of the three novice conditions under the point-cloud policy (46.3%) to the strongest under the keypoint policy (57.3%), a gain of +11.0 percentage points in all five seeds. Those collected with all keypoints emphasized changed by at most +0.7 percentage points, and in no more than three seeds. The value of a demonstration therefore depends on the rendering shown during collection and on what the policy observes together. A shared representation can pay off on both sides, in the number of successful demonstrations and in the success rate of the policy trained on them. Project page: https://omron-sinicx.github.io/point-hand/
authors: Amane Yamaguchi
Shohei Kamiguchi
Masashi Hamaya
Shigeo Yoshida
Takuji Narumi
Mai Nishimura
bullets: The study examines how robot-hand rendering affects novice demonstrations and downstream imitation learning.
PointHand renders a multi-fingered hand as fingertip and joint keypoints, matching the policy’s hand observations.
In a simulated mug-in-box task, novices shown thumb-and-index emphasis produced more successful demonstrations than those shown the real hand shape.
Diffusion policies using keypoint observations benefited most from demonstrations collected with the matching thumb-and-index rendering, improving from 46.3% to 57.3% success within 400 steps.
The findings are limited to a simulated task, a specific teleoperation interface, and the tested renderings and keypoint-based policy observations.
papers.selection_reason: Studies how teleoperation rendering affects demonstrations and downstream diffusion-policy learning, directly relevant to imitation learning and robot manipulation.
papers.title: What Novice Operators See Changes What the Policy Learns: A User Study of Keypoint Hand Visual Representation for Teleoperated Demonstration
papers.tldr: A shared keypoint representation can improve both novice teleoperation demonstrations and the policies trained from them.

papers.abstract: Embodied VLMs can execute increasingly complex manipulation tasks, yet execution errors can leave the environment in states that require replanning for recovery. Existing recovery methods either rely on inference-time mechanisms with fixed policies or learn from failure examples and reference corrections rather than verified action outcomes. To enable recovery learning through verifiable interaction, we introduce the Embodied Replanning for Recovery Environment (ERR-Env), which provides feedback on task progress and execution errors. We further construct ERR-Bench, a benchmark with held-out tasks spanning nominal, intermediate, and error states for evaluating recovery capability and execution reliability. We then propose Action-Grouped Turn-GSPO (AGT-GSPO), an online reinforcement learning method combining turn-level rewards for task progress and error states with action-grouped advantage estimation, and use it to train ERR-VLM, a compact 2B embodied VLM. Evaluation on ERR-Bench reveals a mismatch between task progress and execution reliability across diverse VLMs. AGT-GSPO improves ERR-VLM by 10.25 percentage points in Strict Success Rate for error-free completion and 22.95 percentage points in Recovery Rate, while ablations and zero-shot transfer further validate the effectiveness of our method.
authors: Zhuoran Wang
Keqing Fan
Yang Li

Ke Wang

bullets: Introduces ERR-Env, which provides feedback on task progress and execution errors for recovery learning.
Introduces ERR-Bench with held-out nominal, intermediate, and error-state tasks to evaluate recovery and execution reliability.
Proposes Action-Grouped Turn-GSPO, combining turn-level progress/error rewards with action-grouped advantage estimation.
Trains a compact 2B ERR-VLM; on ERR-Bench, it improves Strict Success Rate by 10.25 points and Recovery Rate by 22.95 points.
Finds that task progress and execution reliability can diverge across VLMs; ablations and zero-shot transfer support the method’s effectiveness.
papers.selection_reason: Trains an embodied VLM for manipulation error recovery via online RL, directly fitting robot learning and vision-language-action.
papers.title: Replan for Error Recovery: Training Embodied VLMs through Verifiable Interaction with Action-Grouped Turn-GSPO
papers.tldr: AGT-GSPO trains embodied VLMs to recover from execution errors through verifiable interaction, substantially improving both reliable task completion and recovery.

papers.abstract: Shared autonomy is a control paradigm that combines human cognitive abilities with robot precision to enable effective remote manipulation in complex environments. A key challenge is how to adapt the level of autonomy using information extracted from the human, task, and/or environment. In this paper, we propose a novel arbitration strategy that dynamically adjusts the level of autonomy in the system using the entropy of a belief distribution derived from a multimodal intent inference. Human intent is modeled with a Dynamic Bayesian Network (DBN), which updates beliefs over goals given real-time operator gaze data and robot arm motion during teleoperation. We then formulate the blending of human input and autonomous control as a Model Predictive Control (MPC) problem, where the system's autonomous behavior is guided by the belief distribution. This approach enables continuous, gradual transitions across the full spectrum of autonomy levels, from direct teleoperation to full autonomy. To validate our approach, we conducted experiments to compare the performance of our proposed algorithm against two MPC-based shared autonomy methods. Compared to the baselines, our approach achieved reductions of at least 61% in object retrieval time, 44% in trajectory length, and 60% in human control input. Participants reported high perceived control, predictability, intent recognition, and responsiveness, along with low workload.
authors: Lorena Maria Genua
Camilla Tabasso
Mya Schroder
Joshua Migdal
Tye Brady
Taskin Padir
bullets: Addresses the challenge of choosing the appropriate autonomy level in shared remote manipulation.
Infers operator goals with a Dynamic Bayesian Network from real-time gaze and robot-arm motion.
Uses belief entropy to arbitrate between human commands and autonomous MPC control.
Supports continuous transitions from direct teleoperation to full autonomy.

Compared with two MPC-based baselines, experiments found at least 61% lower retrieval time, 44% shorter trajectories, and 60% less human control input; users also reported strong usability and low workload.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses shared autonomy in remote manipulation by using a Model Predictive Control (MPC) approach guided by human intent inferred from gaze data, contributing to robot manipulation and control strategies.
papers.title: Intent-Informed Model Predictive Control for Shared Autonomy in Remote Manipulation Tasks
papers.tldr: An intent-aware MPC controller uses gaze and arm motion to smoothly adapt autonomy during remote manipulation, improving efficiency while preserving human control.

papers.abstract: Lossless tensor compression could reduce memory usage during training, but training requires tensors to be repeatedly re-encoded. We introduce Losslessly Compressed Tensors (LCT), a GPU execution framework designed for this repeated encode-decode regime. LCT exploits the natural redundancy in floating point data to reduce storage for weights, activations and optimizer states. Highly optimized GPU kernels implement Huffman coding with precomputed codebooks for low compression and decompression overhead, essential for training. Our analysis characterizes LCT's storage costs and adaptation to magnitude shifts. LCT achieves a compression ratio of up to $1.455\times$, and is demonstrated in training and finetuning settings. On a 162M-parameter NanoGPT, LCT reduces memory usage by $24.6\%$ for a $7.2\%$ step-time increase. In Qwen3-4B fine-tuning, LCT saves up to $23.8\%$ of peak memory, enabling a $3.5\times$ larger context length in training on the same GPU.
authors: Max Zhu
Bohang Sun
Pietro Lio
Jialin Yu
bullets: Targets repeated compression and decompression of weights, activations, and optimizer states during training.
Uses GPU-optimized Huffman coding with precomputed codebooks to keep encoding overhead low.
Achieves compression ratios of up to 1.455× and adapts to shifts in tensor magnitudes.
Reduces NanoGPT memory usage by 24.6% with a 7.2% step-time increase.
During Qwen3-4B fine-tuning, saves up to 23.8% peak memory and enables 3.5× longer context on the same GPU.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a GPU-friendly framework for losslessly compressed tensors during training, reducing memory usage by 24.6% while maintaining acceptable step-time overhead, a significant contribution to memory efficiency.
papers.title: LCT: Losslessly Compressed Tensors with GPU friendly execution for Training
papers.tldr: LCT reduces training memory by losslessly compressing tensors with GPU-efficient encode/decode, trading modest runtime overhead for substantially larger context capacity.

papers.abstract: We introduce FORGE (Fast On-chip Rotor Generation for Experts), a procedural weight generation system for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference. Rather than storing and loading every expert weight tensor from HBM, we show how a compact accelerator inside each Streaming Multiprocessor can regenerate them on-the-fly from $O(\log^2 d)$ rotor parameters per projection. Per replaced layer, gigabytes of stored expert weights are approximated with under a megabyte of seeds. This addresses the dual memory bottleneck of autoregressive Sparse MoE decode, where per-expert FFN operations are HBM-bandwidth-bound at small routed-token counts and the aggregate expert footprint forces multi-node Expert Parallelism (EP) with all-to-all traffic. We realize the approach as the Rotor Generation Unit (RGU), a fixed-function datapath that generates FFN weight tiles without competing with Tensor Core execution. With 30% of the MoE FFN layers replaced across five Sparse MoE models, we estimate 1.3-2.8x higher system throughput at matched GPU count and 1.10-1.15x lower per-user decode latency at short context. In exchange, downstream accuracy on three model families falls below that of the same model fine-tuned without rotor replacement, and the replacement ratio controls this tradeoff. FORGE also expands KV cache capacity by 1.2-2.6x. It is agnostic to the bit width at which weights are stored, so it can compose with quantization. The RGU is fully implemented/verified in SystemVerilog at ~0.9% SM area overhead (0.032 mm^2/SM, 7nm).
authors: Chanyoung Moon
Travis Pence
Daisuke Yamada
Jiaqi Mo
Yanxin Zhang
Vikas Singh
Karthikeyan Sankaralingam
bullets: Targets HBM bandwidth bottlenecks and large expert-storage footprints during autoregressive Sparse MoE decode.
Uses a Rotor Generation Unit to generate FFN weight tiles from compact rotor parameters instead of storing full expert tensors.
Replacing 30% of MoE FFN layers is estimated to improve system throughput by 1.3–2.8× and short-context per-user latency by 1.10–1.15×.
Expands KV-cache capacity by 1.2–2.6× and can compose with weight quantization.
The accuracy–efficiency tradeoff depends on the replacement ratio; accuracy decreases relative to fine-tuned models without rotor replacement.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a procedural weight generation system (FORGE) for Sparse MoE inference that reduces memory footprint and expands KV cache capacity, addressing key efficiency bottlenecks in large model deployment.
papers.title: FORGE: Procedural Weight Generation for Sparse MoE Inference
papers.tldr: FORGE accelerates Sparse MoE decoding by regenerating approximate expert weights on-chip, reducing memory and communication demands at the cost of some accuracy.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but remains computationally expensive and sample inefficient. On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision from a stronger teacher, yet standard OPD distills every token regardless of whether the teacher's preference actually improves task reward. Existing token-selection methods rely on proxies such as uncertainty or teacher--student divergence, which need not identify reward-improving supervision. We introduce Reward-Aligned Distillation (RAD), a bilevel framework that weights distillation signals based on their predicted effect on the student's post-update reward. RAD differentiates through a temporary optimizer step to score each token's supervision, then updates the token weights by projected ascent from the initial token weights. The resulting weights can strengthen, suppress, or reverse individual distillation-gradient contributions. At a matched training-response budget, RAD improves mean accuracy on six competition-math benchmarks over the strongest baselines by 6.5 percentage points for Qwen3-1.7B (non-thinking) and 2.5 points for Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. RAD-Simple, a simplified variant, achieves comparable math accuracy at the same training-response budget. On LiveCodeBench-v6, RAD reaches 54.69\% and 58.67\% pass@1 with Qwen3-1.7B (non-thinking) and OLMo3-7B-Instruct, respectively, exceeding the strongest baselines by 8.7 and 6.4 points. These results support reward-guided weighting of teacher supervision across model families and tasks.
authors: Yilan Chen
Zian Su
Manish Prajapat
Dingmin Wang
Rein Houthooft
Rui Song
Vijay Lingam
bullets: Targets the inefficiency of applying teacher guidance to every token, including supervision that may not improve task reward.
Uses a bilevel temporary optimizer step to estimate each token’s reward impact and updates weights through projected ascent.
Token weights can amplify, suppress, or reverse individual distillation-gradient contributions.
At matched training-response budgets, RAD improves competition-math accuracy over strong baselines across tested Qwen3 models and improves LiveCodeBench pass@1 across two model families.
RAD-Simple achieves comparable math accuracy, suggesting the approach can be simplified without major loss.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a bilevel framework for distilling LLMs that aligns token-level supervision with the predicted effect on task reward, offering a novel approach to improving reasoning capabilities in LLM training.
papers.title: Reward-Aligned Distillation
papers.tldr: Reward-Aligned Distillation improves on-policy distillation by weighting teacher supervision according to its predicted impact on the student’s reward.

papers.abstract: Dual-process agents pair a fast policy with a slow deliberative model. In real-time settings the slow model usually runs continuously; in turn-based agents and robot planners it is invoked on events such as uncertainty or a detected failure. We study a fast learned actor that takes every decision and hands control to a reasoning vision-language model only when a gate opens, while the game keeps running. We use closed-loop Doom and the new open "System One" typed-decision models, served through a common llama.cpp interface. On 900 held-out questions, (i) zero-shot decision models from 0.15B to 9B parameters choose to collect items 1.6-1.8 times more often than chance among their errors, in any option order, although the order changes some models' accuracy; (ii) accuracy, calibration and sensitivity (how well confidence separates right from wrong answers) are distinct: models of similar accuracy differ widely in AUROC, and the confidence of the most sensitive one tracks which kinds of situation it fails, not which answers are wrong; (iii) offline, deferring the least confident 30% of decisions to a reasoning model gains over random deferral in proportion to the actor's AUROC (rank correlation 0.87); with actor and rate chosen on held-out games the gain is +0.13 [0.08, 0.18] with doomLaya's option order and +0.08 [0.02, 0.14] with shuffled options, and reasoning carries about half of it; (iv) in closed loop (33 games, three seeds) no variant reaches the exit. Committing to plans, the reasoner's or a fixed explore rule's, opens more doors and makes an actor that stands still play; with the rule the agent dies more often. Told that some doors need keys, the reasoner takes ordinary doors for locked ones, which the state cannot tell apart; without that knowledge it goes back to collecting. We release code, prompts, data and logs.
authors: Gian Luca Bailo
bullets: The system combines a fast actor with a reasoning vision-language model that takes over when a confidence gate opens while the game continues.
Across 900 held-out questions, confidence quality—not accuracy alone—predicts the benefit of deferring decisions to the reasoning model.
Deferring the least-confident 30% outperforms random deferral offline, with gains correlated strongly with the actor’s AUROC; reasoning accounts for about half the gain.
In 33 closed-loop games across three seeds, no variant reached the exit, exposing failures in planning, exploration, and distinguishing locked from ordinary doors.
The authors release code, prompts, data, and logs.
papers.selection_reason: Studies a dual-process agent architecture (fast actor + slow VLM) in a closed-loop game environment, exploring the decision boundary for when to invoke reasoning, which is relevant to Vision-Language-Action models.
papers.title: System Switch: When Should a Fast Decision Model Stop and Think?
papers.tldr: A fast decision model can use confidence-based gating to selectively invoke slower reasoning, but this strategy shows offline promise and fails to reliably complete the closed-loop Doom task.

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) reduces the cost of adapting foundation models by focusing training on a small parameter subset. Complementary to this idea, we introduce RoSA (Rotational Sparse Adaptation), which narrows adaptation to a subset of layers at a time. RoSA freezes lower layers close to the input throughout training and rotates a trainable block over later layers, progressively increasing the number of frozen layers close to the input. This design reduces optimizer-state memory, shortens backpropagation, and even forward propagation if activations at the last frozen layer are cached. Because RoSA is orthogonal to the choice of trainable parameterization, it can be combined with PEFT methods or sparse optimizers within each active block. Experiments across multiple LLM architectures and tasks show that RoSA reduces peak memory while maintaining strong fine-tuning performance.
authors: Muhammad Azeem Lodhi
Chao Zhou
Rebekka Burkholz
bullets: Targets the memory and computational costs of adapting foundation models.
Freezes lower, input-near layers and shifts the trainable block across later layers during training.
Can reduce optimizer-state memory, backpropagation cost, and—when activations are cached—forward-propagation cost.
Works alongside PEFT methods and sparse optimizers within each active block.
Experiments across multiple LLM architectures and tasks report lower peak memory with strong fine-tuning performance.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a memory-efficient fine-tuning method (RoSA) that reduces optimizer-state memory and computation by freezing layers and rotating trainable blocks, directly addressing memory bottlenecks in LLM training.
papers.title: RoSA: Rotational Sparse Adaptation for Memory-Efficient Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: RoSA reduces fine-tuning memory and computation by rotating a trainable layer block through later layers while progressively freezing earlier ones.

papers.abstract: Deployed LLM agents increasingly rely on persistent, versioned system assets such as routing rules, knowledge segments, prompt instructions, and reusable skills. Failure-localization methods can identify where an error manifests in an agent or execution trace, but repair requires a different decision: which editable system asset should be changed, and is that change expected to improve the task outcome? We study this gap through component-attribute failure attribution, where diagnosis targets versioned, addressable items rather than execution locations. We propose the Detection-Aware Attribution Framework (DAAF), which learns the effects of valid attribute replacements and amortizes this intervention evidence into deployment-time diagnosis. DAAF combines sparse and noisy failure signals to decide whether intervention is warranted, learns component-type-conditioned replacement effects from controlled replays evaluated by executable task outcomes, and shares supervision across requests with compatible intervention responses. At diagnosis time, DAAF uses only the observed execution, registered candidates, and available failure signals; it requires neither counterfactual replay nor task reward and returns no_change, a repair target, or an unresolved decision when evidence is insufficient. On held-out tau^2-bench Telecom tasks, DAAF achieves 80.72% attribute Hit@1, recovers 62.65% of failed executions while limiting clean-task regression to 3.23%, and reaches 71.93% overall task success. These results show that intervention-grounded attribute attribution can connect failure localization to executable system repair.
authors: Xiaoyang Yuan
Qi Liu
Yubin Ruan
Xinyi Mou
Zhuomeng Zhang
Wenjin Wang
Hanying Jiao
Di Wu
Mingye Xu
Yi Bin
Ke Feng
Zixun Sun
bullets: Targets versioned, addressable assets such as routing rules, knowledge segments, prompts, and reusable skills rather than execution locations.
Learns component-specific replacement effects from controlled replays and combines sparse, noisy failure signals across compatible requests.
At deployment, diagnoses from the observed execution, registered candidates, and failure signals without counterfactual replay or task reward.
On held-out tau^2-bench Telecom tasks, achieves 80.72% attribute Hit@1, recovers 62.65% of failures, and reaches 71.93% overall task success.
Limits clean-task regression to 3.23% and can return no_change or unresolved when evidence is insufficient.
papers.selection_reason: Focuses on LLM agents and the technical challenge of diagnosing and repairing system assets (routing rules, knowledge segments) at deployment time, which falls under the scope of LLM agent research.
papers.title: DAAF: From Failure Localization to Editable System Assets in LLM Agents
papers.tldr: DAAF identifies which editable LLM-agent system asset should be changed—and when no change is warranted—using intervention evidence learned from controlled replays.

papers.abstract: Current Transformer interfaces index tokens by one or more integer coordinates, which determine their addresses inside attention. In RoPE and its multi-axis or hierarchical variants, the resulting address has the form $A(i)=R_1^{i_1}R_2^{i_2}R_3^{i_3}$, where the exponents are integer coordinates assigned after choosing a serialized token layout. When Transformers process new or large collections of data, this addressing scheme can produce unseen offsets or coordinate combinations, push repositories toward retrieve-and-serialize pipelines, and force new entities, records, or repository items to be represented by long token strings or identifier embeddings not seen in training. We introduce labeled incidence structures (LIS), in which each participating token or value is an endpoint with content $x$ and a structural index $i$. The index can include local position, relation role, relation instance, text unit, field, or content-derived identity. The model maps this index to a structural address $A(i)$, so adding new tokens, facts, text units, or repository items applies the same learned address rule to structural and content coordinates rather than requiring larger integer coordinates, unseen coordinate combinations, or new identifier embeddings. Attention scores endpoints $i,j$ using $q_i^\top P_{j\to i}k_j$, where journey consistency forces $P_{j\to i}=A(i)^{-1}A(j)$. When $i$ has several coordinates, such as position, role, and instance, coordinate independence is equivalent to factoring $A(i)$ into one address factor per coordinate. This recovers RoPE, RoPE-2D, and HiRoPE as special cases. This allows knowledge-graph (KG) roles, fact instances, and text units to enter the attention score directly. In controlled shallow diagnostics, the LIS address interface is implemented inside ordinary Transformer attention and yields promising results across text, KG, and $n$-ary settings.
authors: Mahesh Godavarti
bullets: Transformers can struggle with unseen offsets, coordinate combinations, and newly introduced entities or repository items.
LIS represents each token or value by content plus a multi-coordinate structural index, such as position, role, relation instance, or text unit.
Attention uses journey-consistent structural transformations, with coordinate factorization recovering RoPE, RoPE-2D, and HiRoPE as special cases.
The interface can incorporate knowledge-graph roles, fact instances, and text units directly into attention rather than relying on retrieve-and-serialize pipelines.
Controlled shallow diagnostics report promising results across text, knowledge-graph, and n-ary settings, though the abstract does not establish broader performance or scalability.
papers.selection_reason: A native Transformer indexing and addressing framework extends LLM architecture reasoning beyond standard positional encodings.
papers.title: Labeled Incidence Structures for Native Transformer Modeling of Text, Knowledge Graphs, and Hypergraphs
papers.tldr: Labeled incidence structures (LIS) extend Transformer positional addressing to directly represent structural roles, relations, instances, and identities across text, knowledge graphs, and hypergraphs.

papers.abstract: Safety-critical driving scenario generation has largely focused on manipulating the behavior of surrounding agents while starting from an initial scene from driving data. This assumption can limit the space of discoverable failures, since driving data can provide little opportunity for meaningful interaction. For example, in the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, 20.44% of recorded slices feature a stationary ego vehicle that never moves, and 30.39% of initial frames contain no nearby traffic participants within 10 meters. We instead study safety-critical scenario generation as an initialization problem: given agnostic black-box driving policies, we learn to generate realistic initial scenes that are more likely to evolve into critical interactions. We propose AdvScene, a conditional latent diffusion model that is trained in two stages. Starting from pretraining on naturalistic driving data, we post-train the adversarial-agent generation branch using reinforcement learning with feedback from closed-loop simulator rollouts. Conditioning on ego driving displacement prevents the ego from remaining static, and RL finetuning induces criticality directly with non-differentiable safety-critical metrics. Experiments on the Waymo dataset across 12 combinations of ego and traffic policies show that our AdvScene substantially increases the rate of ego-fault collision events and TTC<3s events.
authors: Yin Wu
Jiarong Wei
Carl Esselborn
Shubham Phoolari
Ahmed Abouelazm
Daniel Slieter
J. Marius Zöllner
bullets: Existing methods mainly manipulate surrounding agents from fixed data-derived scenes, limiting discoverable failures.
AdvScene treats scenario generation as an initialization problem and uses a conditional latent diffusion model.
It pretrains on naturalistic driving data, then uses reinforcement learning with closed-loop simulator feedback.
Ego displacement conditioning avoids static ego vehicles, while RL directly optimizes non-differentiable safety metrics.
Across 12 ego–traffic policy combinations on Waymo, it increases ego-fault collisions and TTC<3s events.
papers.selection_reason: Learned safety-critical driving scene generation for embodied policies is relevant to embodied-agent evaluation and transferable to learned navigation testing.
papers.title: Safety-Critical Scenarios Emerge from Initial Scenes
papers.tldr: AdvScene generates realistic initial driving scenes that more often lead black-box policies into safety-critical interactions.

papers.abstract: Placing a grasped book into a tight shelf is a compact but difficult contact-rich control problem: millimetre-scale pose error can turn a geometrically valid approach into jamming, failed release, or incomplete seating. We study this final phase after grasp acquisition and global approach, and ask how control authority should be divided between known geometry and learned behaviour. Our method retains a nominal task-space controller for structured insertion and seating, while residual PPO supplies bounded local corrections and decides when to release. Only the brief open-retreat-reclose transition is scripted. For the final policy used on hardware, a deployment-matched simulation evaluation over 512 fixed conditions yields 98.50 percent mean success (0.23 percentage-point sample SD) across three independent training runs, compared with 37.89 percent for nominal control. On the physical xArm7, 60 trials over 30 matched conditions show the same qualitative advantage: residual control raises success from 26.7 percent to 63.3 percent, reduces failures from 22 to 11, and wins 13 of the 15 matched conditions in which the two controllers differ. Robustness tests show that performance remains above 87 percent under initialization perturbations up to 1.5x, while very tight clearances expose the geometric limit of local correction. These results support a hybrid design in which geometry preserves reliable task structure and learning is concentrated on the contact-sensitive behaviour that fixed rules handle poorly.
authors: Tianyuan Liu
Rutherford Agbeshi Patamia
Benjamin Champion
Akansel Cosgun
Richard Dazeley
bullets: Targets the final shelf-insertion phase, where millimetre-scale pose errors can cause jamming, failed release, or incomplete seating.
Keeps a nominal task-space controller for structured motion and seating; bounded residual PPO handles local contact corrections and release timing.
Only the brief open-retreat-reclose transition is scripted, concentrating learning on contact-sensitive behavior.
In simulation, residual control achieves 98.50% mean success versus 37.89% for nominal control; on an xArm7, success increases from 26.7% to 63.3%.
Performance remains above 87% under initialization perturbations up to 1.5×, but very tight clearances exceed the method’s local-correction capability.
papers.selection_reason: Residual reinforcement learning for contact-rich manipulation is a direct robot learning contribution.
papers.title: Hybrid Residual Reinforcement Learning for Contact-Rich Robotic Book Insertion
papers.tldr: A hybrid controller combining geometric insertion with learned residual corrections greatly improves contact-rich book placement, while retaining limitations under very tight clearances.

papers.abstract: A geometrically valid placement can still be difficult to execute because the selected grasp changes the required end-effector pose, collision geometry, and transport motion. Placement is formulated as a pre-execution ranking problem in which supplied grasp-placement candidates are scored before planning. The model combines a typed target-conditioned point cloud with three pose descriptors and hierarchical heads for planning success and execution success conditioned on planning. On a 30-object, 1,235-scene dataset with scene-group-held-out splits, three-seed top-1 success on covered test groups reaches 85.63 +/- 1.08% for joint selection and 79.84 +/- 0.16% for fixed-target ranking. For the designated frozen seed-42 checkpoint, top-1 success improves from 72.84% to 85.78% over full-pool cuMotion for joint ranking and from 59.65% to 79.67% for fixed-target ranking. Frozen transfer to xArm7/MoveIt requires no xArm-specific retraining. Across 27 locked cases, 13 complete end to end (48.15%). Of the 16 cases that pass Top-5 preflight and begin execution, 13 succeed (81.25%). Candidate-level deployment-feasibility prediction reaches 81.25% recall, 85.20% specificity, and 83.23% balanced accuracy.
authors: Tianyuan Liu
Rutherford Agbeshi Patamia
Benjamin Champion
Richard Dazeley
Akansel Cosgun
bullets: Addresses the gap between geometric placement validity and practical execution difficulty caused by grasp-dependent poses, collisions, and transport motions.
Uses a target-conditioned point cloud with three pose descriptors and hierarchical heads predicting planning success and execution success conditioned on planning.
On covered test groups, top-1 success reaches 85.63% for joint grasp-placement selection and 79.84% for fixed-target ranking.
The frozen seed-42 model improves over full-pool cuMotion from 72.84% to 85.78% for joint ranking and from 59.65% to 79.67% for fixed-target ranking.
Transfer to xArm7/MoveIt requires no xArm-specific retraining; 13 of 16 Top-5-preflight cases succeed during execution.
papers.selection_reason: Grasp-conditioned placement ranking improves robot manipulation and execution feasibility, fitting learned manipulation research.
papers.title: Execution-Aware Pre-Execution Ranking for Grasp-Conditioned Robotic Placement
papers.tldr: Ranks grasp-conditioned placement candidates before motion planning to favor placements that are both geometrically valid and executable.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robot learning, with performance improving as models and datasets scale. Scaling robot data collection, however, remains challenging because data are naturally distributed across robots, tasks, and locations, making centralization costly or impractical. Federated learning offers a way to train on decentralized robot data, but applying it to VLAs requires accounting for heterogeneous robot client data distributions. We present Co-VLA, which applies consensus optimization using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers~(ADMM) to federated VLA training. We show that the same algorithm supports both full-model training and parameter-efficient fine-tuning with both fixed-rank and rank-adaptive adapters. The name Co-VLA reflects both consensus and collaboration: clients with different local robot datasets collaboratively train a shared model without sharing their data. Our experiments demonstrate that Co-VLA achieves performance comparable to centralized training in both full-model training and parameter-efficient fine-tuning settings. The project website and videos of our real-world experiments are available at https://embodiedvision.github.io/co-vla/.
authors: Haolong Li
Guner Dilsad Er
Michael Muehlebach
Joerg Stueckler
bullets: Addresses the challenge of scaling robot data collection when data are distributed across robots, tasks, and locations.
Applies consensus optimization with the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to federated VLA training.
Supports both full-model training and parameter-efficient fine-tuning with fixed-rank and rank-adaptive adapters.
Experiments show performance comparable to centralized training in both training settings.
Scope: designed for heterogeneous client data while keeping local robot data private to each client.
papers.selection_reason: Training vision-language-action models with federated consensus directly targets VLA policy learning and robot manipulation.
papers.title: Co-VLA: Consensus-based Federated Training for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: Co-VLA uses ADMM-based consensus optimization to train vision-language-action models collaboratively across heterogeneous robots without centralizing their data.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models have achieved remarkable progress in multi-modal understanding, yet their capabilities in educational settings remain insufficiently evaluated. In AI-assisted language learning, models must interpret artistic imagery, understand its semantic, affective, and cultural content, and reason about visual context to support meaningful interaction. However, existing benchmarks primarily focus on real-world images or domain-specific educational reasoning, providing limited coverage of artistic educational content. To address this gap, we introduce MUSE, a benchmark for evaluating large vision-language models on artistic image understanding in situated educational applications. MUSE decouples image annotation from question generation, enabling diverse tasks with controllable difficulty while reducing annotation effort. It comprises twelve tasks spanning visual perception, semantic and affective interpretation, culture understanding, and compositional reasoning, together with diverse artistic images deliberately curated to center Singaporean and Southeast Asian multicultural contexts alongside Western art traditions, covering multiple themes and difficulty levels. Evaluation of open-source and proprietary models reveals substantial disparities across capability dimensions, particularly in affective interpretation and compositional reasoning. Our analysis further identifies common failure modes and key challenges for developing trustworthy multi-modal models for education. We hope MUSE will serve as a standardized benchmark for advancing multi-modal understanding in situated educational applications.
authors: Luyao Zhu
Xun Wei Yee
Wei Li
Mun Thye Mak
Wee Siong Ng
bullets: Addresses limited evaluation of multimodal models on artistic content in education, especially language-learning contexts.
Separates image annotation from question generation to support diverse, controllable-difficulty tasks with lower annotation effort.
Covers 12 tasks spanning visual perception, semantic and affective interpretation, cultural understanding, and compositional reasoning.
Includes multicultural artistic imagery centered on Singaporean and Southeast Asian contexts alongside Western art traditions.
Finds substantial capability gaps, especially in affective interpretation and compositional reasoning, and analyzes common failure modes.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark evaluating large vision-language models on multimodal artistic-image understanding, directly relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: MUSE: Benchmarking Large Vision-Language Models on Multi-Modal Understanding in Situated Education
papers.tldr: MUSE benchmarks large vision-language models on artistic image understanding for culturally situated educational applications.
